title: Why a 1 TB drive shows up as 931 GB
summary: Drive makers count in powers of ten, computers often in powers of two. One trillion bytes is about 931 gibibytes.

beats.say: A one terabyte drive can read as nine hundred thirty one gigabytes.
beats.cap: 1 TB on the box. 931 GB on screen.

beats.say: Nothing is missing. The two sides count in different units.
Drive makers count in powers of ten. A gigabyte is a billion bytes.
Some systems count in powers of two, and still say gigabytes.
To the drive maker, a terabyte is exactly one trillion bytes.
A trillion bytes, divided into computer gigabytes, is nine hundred thirty one.
No bytes vanish. The drive holds one trillion either way.
It is a naming problem, not a storage problem.
The fix is a separate unit with its own name: the gibibyte.
One trillion bytes. Nine hundred thirty one gibibytes.

claims.note: Wikipedia, Tera-: tera equals 10^12, the integer 1,000,000,000,000

facts.claim: NIST defines the gibibyte as 2^30 bytes, 1,073,741,824 bytes
facts.note: NIST binary-prefix page: 1 GiB = 2^30 B = 1 073 741 824 B; 1 GB = 10^9 B

facts.claim: Drive makers use decimal prefixes, and a drive marketed as 1 TB could be reported as 931 GB
facts.note: Wikipedia, Binary prefix: manufacturers always used decimal SI prefixes; 'a hard drive marketed as 1 TB could be reported as having only 931 GB'

facts.claim: Some operating systems still use GB to denote binary multiples
facts.note: Wikipedia, Binary prefix: some programs and operating systems, such as Microsoft Windows, still use MB and GB for binary prefixes

facts.claim: The IEC adopted binary prefixes such as gibi to remove the ambiguity
facts.note: Wikipedia, Tera-: the IEC adopted tebi- to signify 2^40 and avoid the ambiguity

youtube.hook: A 1 TB drive holds one trillion bytes. A computer that counts in powers of two reports that as about 931 GiB. Nothing is missing, the two sides use different units.
